articles.title: On This Day, Oct. 13: Continental Congress establishes Navy

paras.en: Oct. 13 (UPI) -- On this date in history:
In 1775, the Continental Congress ordered construction of America's first naval fleet.
In 1792, the cornerstone to the White House in Washington was laid. It would be November 1800 before the first presidential family -- that of John Adams -- moved in.
In 1903, the Boston Americans (later known as the Red Sox) beat the Pittsburgh Pirates to win the first modern World Series, five games to three.
In 1917, up to 100,000 people gathered in Fatima, Portugal, for the "Miracle of the Sun" and its strange solar activity and, for many, a reported glimpse of the Virgin Mary.
In 1943, conquered by the Allies, Italy declared war on Germany, its Axis former partner.

In 1972, Uruguayan Air Force Flight 571 carrying 45 people, including a rugby team from Montevideo, crashed in the Andes mountains. It would take 72 days for rescuers to learn the fate of the survivors, and by that time, only 16 were left to tell their story. The survivor's harrowing story was brought to the big screen in the 1993 feature film, Alive.
In 1972, more than 170 people were killed in a Soviet airliner crash near Moscow's Sheremetyevo International Airport.

In 1987, Costa Rican President Oscar Arias Sanchez was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize -- the first winner from Central America. Arias was recognized for his work promoting democracy and peace in Central America.
In 1990, Syrian forces moved into Lebanon, removing Christian militia leader General Michel Aoun from power, effectively ending the Lebanese Civil War.

In 1994, two months after the Irish Republican Army announced a cease-fire, the Ulster Volunteer Force and Ulster Freedom Fighters, the two main paramilitary groups fighting to keep Northern Ireland with its Protestant majority in the United Kingdom, announced a cease-fire.

In 2000, the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the Nobel Peace Prize to South Korean President Kim Dae-jung for his efforts to reconcile his country with North Korea through a summit earlier in the year with counterpart Kim Jong Il.

In 2010, after more than two months entombed half a mile under the Chilean desert, the first of 33 trapped miners was pulled to safety in a narrow passageway drilled through more than 2,000 feet of rock, to be followed in the next 24 hours by the rest of the crew in a dramatic finale to a remarkable rescue mission.

In 2013, a stampede by masses of worshipers crossing a bridge over the Sindh River at a Hindu festival in India's Madhya Pradesh state killed more than 100 people and injured scores of others. A police official said people panicked as rumors spread that the bridge was collapsing.
In 2019, American Simone Biles became the most decorated gymnast in history with her record 25th gold medal at the World Championships in Stuttgart, Germany.
In 2021, Star Trek actor William Shatner, at 90, became the oldest person to go to space. He traveled with three others aboard a Blue Origin capsule and returned 11 minutes after reaching space.
In 2024, SpaceX used a tower with arms to "catch" the 20-story-tall booster for its Starship rocket for the first time.

articles.title: A$AP Rocky Announces First Australian and New Zealand Tour in Eight Years
articles.author: Jessica Lynch

paras.en: A$AP Rocky is returning to Australia and New Zealand. The rapper has announced a five-date arena tour for December, his first visit to the region in eight years.

The local leg of his Don’t Be Dumb World Tour opens Dec. 5 at Melbourne’s Rod Laver Arena, followed by Sydney’s Afterpay Arena on Dec. 9, Auckland’s Spark Arena on Dec. 12, Brisbane Entertainment Centre on Dec. 14 and Perth’s RAC Arena on Dec. 17. Tickets go on general sale Friday, Oct. 16 at 1 p.m. local time, following artist, Vodafone, Mastercard, Live Nation and Westfield presales earlier in the week.

The dates follow a sold-out 25-date run across the U.K. and Europe that saw Rocky perform in 19 countries. According to promoter Live Nation, the European leg broke several regional records, including the fastest-selling rap show in Greece and the biggest arena sales for a rap artist in Zagreb, Belgrade and Sofia.

The tour supports Don’t Be Dumb, released in January as the long-awaited follow-up to 2018’s Testing. The album debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 — Rocky’s third chart-topper and his first in more than a decade — moving 123,000 equivalent album units in its opening week, and also topped Australia’s ARIA Hip-Hop/R&B Albums chart. Its lead single “Punk Rocky” reached No. 9 on Billboard’s Hot Rock & Alternative Songs chart, and the record featured a sprawling guest list including Tyler, the Creator, Doechii, Gorillaz, Brent Faiyaz, Thundercat and will.i.am, with cover artwork created by filmmaker Tim Burton.

articles.title: Jack Johnson Brings His Swell Season to the Hollywood Bowl
articles.author: Darah Head

paras.en: It was homecoming weekend across the Southland, and Jack Johnson and his team brought their A-game to the Hollywood Bowl on Saturday for night one of two sold-out shows: “Y’all came ready to sing, right?”

As Tropical Storm Rachel swirled off the coast, Johnson and his band treated L.A. to a collection of the singer-songwriter’s greatest hits for the final shows of his North American tour in support of SURFILMUSIC, an intimate documentary directed by Emmett Malloy chronicling Johnson’s evolution from surfer to filmmaker to musician.

Underneath a balmy, occasionally drizzly night sky, the laid-back 51-year-old delivered two hours of classic hits accompanied by his longtime band — which includes standout sidekick Zach Gill, who met Johnson during their early days at UC Santa Barbara and accompanies the rocker on everything from accordion and harmonica to piano and melodica — as surf footage and family videos provided a beachside backdrop.

For those of us in college when Johnson rose to prominence, it was a nostalgic night for the mostly Gen X crowd, as our own kids are applying to college these days. But middle age looks good on Johnson, and his commitment to the hits delivered a wave of feel-good moments throughout the quasi-beach party.

Johnson dove right in with “Mudfootball (For Moe Lerner),” from his 2001 debut studio album, Brushfire Fairytales, followed by “Sitting, Waiting, Wishing”; “Bubble Toes” (with a respective intro/outro of the Steve Miller Band’s “Keep on Rockin’ Me Baby” and “Take the Money and Run”); “Banana Pancakes,” followed by a soulful cover of Dolly Parton’s “9 to 5”; “You and Your Heart”; a stripped-down “Breakdown” (with Johnson’s vocals soaring alongside his trademark ukulele); “Upside Down”; “Staple It Together”; “Wasting Time”; “Constellations”; and “Do You Remember.” “Holes to Heaven,” Johnson’s 2003 song about a father-son bonding trip, resonated with the chorus, “And there were so many fewer questions / When stars were still just the holes to heaven.”

paras.en: Longtime friend Ben Harper joined Johnson onstage for “Flake” and a cover of The Wailers’ “High Tide or Low Tide,” and fellow surfer Kelly Slater surfaced for a cover of Jimmy Buffet’s “A Pirate Looks at Forty,” just two guys trading verses back and forth late night on a beach.
The encore of “Better Together,” very likely a first-dance wedding song for many in the crowd, was a fitting reminder that, yes, we are.

Opener Hermanos Gutiérrez, a Latin instrumental duo formed in 2015 in Zurich by Ecuadorian-Swiss brothers Alejandro Gutiérrez and Estevan Gutiérrez, ably set the tone with soulful instrumentals, including the sweet slides of lap steel guitar. The brothers accompanied Johnson on the score to SURFILMUSIC — which premiered March 13 at SXSW and is now screening at select theaters nationwide — and joined the singer onstage for a mashup of songs from the soundtrack.

articles.title: ‘Breaking Bad’ Stars Bryan Cranston, Aaron Paul, Others Remember R.J. Mitte: “Sweetheart of a Young Man”
articles.author: Carly Thomas

paras.en: R.J. Mitte‘s Breaking Bad co-stars are paying tribute to the actor after he died at age 34.

Mitte, who was diagnosed with cerebral palsy as a child and later became a disability rights advocate, died Monday in Brownsville, Texas, his reps previously shared. No cause of death was revealed, but TMZ reported that he died by suicide.

One of his most notable roles was playing Walter White Jr., the son of Bryan Cranston and Anna Gunn’s characters, Walter and Skyler White, on Vince Gilligan’s Breaking Bad. The Emmy-winning series ran for five seasons, from 2008 to 2013.

Earlier this month, Mitte made an appearance on The Joe Vulpis Podcast, where he praised working with Cranston and Gunn on the crime drama. “Bryan and Anna, they have such a wealth of knowledge and have been working in the industry for many years at the time and even more now,” he recalled. “And so every day, as far as it being a dark show having heavy themes, everything was very light-hearted, even in between takes.”
Following the news of Mitte’s death, Cranston, Aaron Paul and Dean Norris are among those remembering the actor.

“I’m in deep despair as I write this tonight,” Cranston shared in a lengthy post on Instagram “RJ Mitte, my sweet son on Breaking Bad has died. I met him when he was only 14 years old when he was cast as Walter White Jr., a part he played with such joy and enthusiasm. Born with Cerebral Palsy, he never – ever – allowed that challenge to be an excuse for anything. He met the demanding shooting schedule head on with great determination. Always listening to the advice that his TV parents (Anna Gunn and myself) gave him – but being a teenager, sometimes mischievously ignoring the counsel in order to learn the hard way… He was one of the stars of a hit TV show – but still a kid.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: He continued, “That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot in February of 2007, but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor. He parlayed his experience on the show to be a vocal advocate for performers with disabilities, and was the head of a philanthropic organization with a focus on helping the disabled community. All that promise and potential now is such a loss. It is especially devastating to hear that he took his own life. Why? We were texting each other just a few weeks ago – figuring out when we could meet for lunch. I don’t know if that lunch would have changed his future… But I do know that I loved him, and thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight on Breaking Bad dimmed… I’ll miss you, son.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “I can’t stop there without imploring anyone who is contemplating suicide to please call for the support you need at 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (https://988lifeline.org/). There is hope,” Cranston concluded.

Paul, who played Jesse Pinkman, also wrote in a statement shared with The Hollywood Reporter, “I am at a loss. I am heartbroken over this news. RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed. And to whoever happens to be reading this, please know you are loved, and you are not alone. Always remember that.”

Norris, who played Hank Schrader, the uncle to Walt Jr., shared, “Though RJ didn’t play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set. He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed. This is so heartbreaking, I can’t believe it. Thinking of him and his family.”

articles.title: ‘Tyson’ Review: Netflix’s Docuseries Tells Mike Tyson’s Story as Only Mike Tyson Could Tell It, and Already Has Several Times
articles.author: Daniel Fienberg

paras.en: Of all the contradictions that make up Mike Tyson‘s public persona, none causes me to scratch my head as much as this: Tyson‘s entire ethos could be boiled down to not caring what “people” — the mainstream in general, but the media in particular — think of him, but no figure of his stature has put in the conspicuous and shameless effort to make sure that anybody whose residency is not beneath a rock has heard Tyson’s version of who he is.

He has been the focal point of an Animal Planet documentary about himself and his love of pigeons (Taking on Tyson) and the centerpiece of an Adult Swim animated series about himself and, well, his love of pigeons (Mike Tyson Mysteries). He had a long-running one-man show about his life (I assume pigeons were involved, but I don’t remember). Even when Hulu made a limited series about his life — 2022’s Mike, which couldn’t have made less of a cultural footprint — and Tyson threw a tantrum comparing Hulu to a slave master, that unauthorized version of Tyson’s story was completely interchangeable with the authorized version he has told so many times.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: I suspect this simultaneous desire to be represented and professed antipathy at being represented isn’t an unreasonable facet of the celebrity condition, and that if somebody were to ask him why he can’t stop telling his own story, one viable answer would be “money” — which is probably reasonable as well.

I assume Tyson wasn’t paid for his central role in Floyd Russ’ Netflix docuseries Tyson, and he isn’t even an executive producer on the four-parter. But it’s only ever the version of Mike Tyson’s story that he wants it to be — candid and emotionally raw one moment, stubbornly and annoyingly evasive the next.

Russ never directly asks Tyson what he hopes to get out of appearing in the project, which makes it clear that for all the objectionable and illegal behavior that have been part of Tyson’s life, he has never been “cancelled,” so to speak. He was out of the public eye for a couple of years when he was serving prison time for rape, and the tone of the conversation may have briefly darkened in the few months after he repeatedly bit Evander Holyfield in the ring, but Tyson has retained his position in mainstream culture better than nearly any figure with a comparable rap sheet.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That, ultimately, is what Russ’ docuseries is about. If you were already fascinated by Mike Tyson, Tyson is four hours of storytelling so aesthetically formulaic that it borders on parody, and I don’t think it will provide much new information or even fresh perspective, since Tyson has already given his perspective endlessly. Yet Tyson’s vulnerable volatility is hard to look away from, and Tyson is as well — especially since most people who are grossed out by the excessive platforming of this severely damaged pugilist probably won’t watch anyway.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: A plot summary for curious viewers thinking, “Finally, this will be my opportunity to learn something about that guy from The Hangover“: Russ traces the established facts of Tyson’s life from his rough-and-tumble youth in Brooklyn to his juvenile run-ins with the law to the youth facility where he discovered boxing and which, in turn, connected him to legendary trainer Cus D’Amato.

I’m a big enough boxing fan that I have to admit I’ve watched videos of most of Tyson’s fights, some many times (you could watch his knockout of Michael Spinks nearly 40 times per hour if you chose to); I know it’s hard to look away from the run of vicious stoppages that led to his becoming the youngest heavyweight champion ever.

Russ follows the rise and fall and rise and fall of Tyson’s boxing career to a certain point, interspersing the rape trial, the misadventures of Tyson’s Holyfield fights, the tragic death of his daughter, his drug addiction and recovery and relapses and more. Nothing is exactly off-limits, but most things are governed by when Tyson wants to be forthcoming and when he threateningly looks at the director and urges him to find another line of questioning, which he does a number of times. He’ll talk about his ill-fated marriage to Robin Givens, acknowledging some levels of abuse while avoiding confirmation of others, but when it comes to the Indianapolis rape accusation, one-sentence denials are all you’ll get. Since Givens and Desiree Washington either declined to appear or didn’t respond to requests to appear, what Tyson says goes.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Tyson is at once scary, funny, personable, distasteful, introspective, superficial, articulate and incoherent. He cackles at things a decent person absolutely shouldn’t be cackling at and he’s reduced to conveying wordless sorrow multiple times per episode. I suppose if you’ve never watched any of Tyson’s exercises in self-portraiture, you might find his open-wound quality to be revelatory. Yes, Tyson seems to be comfortable talking to Russ, but I’m not sure that Tyson wouldn’t have been equally unfettered in conversation with a bowl of potato salad. Russ leaves in all those scenes of Tyson telling him to change the subject just to show where his limits are.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The documentary isn’t exclusively a conversation with Tyson. Russ has a solid roster of people from different stretches of Tyson’s life, from childhood friends to gym partners to follow boxers to family members to several of the women who didn’t divorce him or accuse him of rape.

There are insightful conversations with the likes of Lennox Lewis and James “Buster” Douglas, whose attempts to explain what it meant for him to beat Tyson just weeks after losing his mother yielded my only emotional response to the docuseries. There are painful and real interviews with Tyson’s children, who highlight the positives and negatives of having Mike Tyson for a father. While many of the more contentious and controversial aspects of his life are presented in one-sided fashion, friend and former manager Rory Holloway’s still-raw sense of betrayal at Tyson firing his entire team is evoked with vivid irritation.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Russ keeps the storytelling very straightforward and very much in keeping with the style that ESPN and HBO sports documentaries have codified over the years. That means that it’s strictly chronological, except for a few times he “hits rewind” and goes back a few days or even hours, usually to no particular advantage. The editing is rudimentary throughout, whether it’s the myriad scenes intercut with footage of fluttering pigeons or the predictable rhythms of stock footage and inserts. There’s a real opportunity in the fourth episode to do something fun, or at least interesting, when Tyson convinces Russ to join him in smoking hallucinatory toad venom, but no flair or flourishes emerge.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Every once in a while an outside observer, almost always journalist and commentator Van Lathan, will say something that could open the door for Tyson to situate its subject as a product of a specific historical moment or in terms of race in America. Tyson, a student of boxing history, surely would have appreciated a deeper discussion of the role of the Black heavyweight champion in culture. But Tyson doesn’t aspire to be OJ: Made in America and it definitely is not.

That is to say that Tyson is not a docuseries that I would recommend purely on its merits to people who think they have no interest in, or desire to listen to, Mike Tyson for four hours. But if you do, I’ll just say that Donald Trump is a more useful talking head here than in Netflix’s Hulk Hogan documentary, with plenty of (predictable) opinions on sexual assault accusations against Tyson and whatnot. Take all of that as you will.

articles.title: World Bank jobs council urges 'crisis-era' employment support measures as IMF warns of AI ‘tsunami’

paras.en: BANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout.

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down.

"People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future."

Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work.

What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said.

That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said.

The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces.

World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them.

The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away."

The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said.

Banga, however, is less pessimistic about the disruption to the job market from AI. "Large language models are estimated probably to create some degree of disruption in jobs in the developed world," he said. "But by the time you get to middle-income countries and lower-middle-income countries, actually, the opportunity from small AI to build jobs and build productivity is enormous," he told CNBC on Tuesday.

AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said.

"Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva.

Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it."
AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training.

articles.title: Visa gets Beijing's green light for bank card business after 40 years of working with China

paras.en: BEIJING — U.S. credit card giant Visa announced Tuesday it had received approval from the People's Bank of China for setting up a bank card clearing business in the country.
The news comes as the U.S. and Chinese presidents plan for their third meeting this year.
"This marks an important milestone toward the company serving China's domestic payments market," Visa said in a statement.

"For more than 40 years, Visa has been an active contributor to China's dynamic payments landscape," Visa CEO Ryan McInerney said. "We look forward to taking the necessary steps in the process, pursuant to the PBOC's regulations, to begin operating domestically in China."

McInerney joined U.S. President Donald Trump's business delegation to Beijing in May and subsequently became chair of the U.S.-China Business Council in June. The Visa CEO also led a trip to Beijing in early September.
"The timing is notable," said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice, The Asia Group.

"Beijing chose to approve visa's license just ahead of the APEC Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen next month, where Xi [Jinping] and Trump are expected to meet again," he said. "The move suggests that Beijing is keen to demonstrate tangible progress for American businesses before Trump's next visit to China."

Trump told Fox News after his Beijing trip in May that he brought up Visa's request to gain China market access. After the summit in September, China said it would approve applications from all foreign financial institutions to operate in the country.
Mainland China has kept a tight grip on its financial sector, favoring domestic players and restricting cross-border capital flows.
Visa previously said it had applied with the PBOC in May 2020 to operate a bank card clearing institution.

The company has worked with Chinese banks for dual-branded cards, for which China's UnionPay processes transactions domestically and Visa processes overseas payments. In January, Visa said the mainland China-issued cards could be linked to Apple Pay for use overseas.
Rival Mastercard's joint venture in China said it started processing payments in 2024 after getting the PBOC's approval to begin bank card clearing preparations in February 2020.
American Express was the first, receiving its processing license in June 2020 after getting the PBOC nod back in 2018.
Mobile pay dominates daily consumer transactions in China, primarily facilitated by Tencent's WeChat and Alibaba-affiliate Ant's Alipay.

articles.title: As 'Cockroach' protests grow over alleged voter fraud, Modi defends India as ‘mother of democracy’

paras.en: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday defended India as a "mother of democracy," as protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter fraud are intensifying.

"A wide range of issues are debated openly, and diverse perspectives are discussed by the people," Modi said, speaking at a Bloomberg New Economy event. His comments coincide with a severe crackdown by authorities against protestors demanding electoral reforms.
Earlier today, a key members of the viral pseudo-political movement, Cockroach Janta Party, were detained for protesting without permission.

CJP, whose leaders were detained by authorities over the weekend as well, had sought permission from Delhi Police on Monday to launch fresh protests at the Jantar Mantar grounds in the capital. However, the government then barred the use of the site for protests.

On Monday, thousands of people reportedly joined leaders of Indian opposition parties in their march to the Supreme Court in Delhi to file a petition against revisions made to the voter list by the Election Commission.

Names of 130 million people have been struck off from the voter list after the commission began conducting "special intensive revisions" (SIR) to update voter lists across the country last year, as per several local media reports.
Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in India, said the huge crowds were a sign that people were not going to be "intimidated" by the government.

"There are no parallel protests. It's one protest, and it's a protest where everybody is standing together," Gandhi said, dismissing concerns over the absence of members of the Cockroach Janta Party who had called for protests over the weekend.

"Delhi is once again flooded with people standing up to save democracy," Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the viral pseudo-political movement, CJP, said in a post, reacting to the crowd amassed for the march led by Gandhi.

Over the weekend, Indian security forces reportedly clamped down on protests in the capital city, detaining young people, several opposition party politicians, YouTubers, lawyers and a few journalists.
The Delhi police, which is under the control of the Indian home ministry, did not respond to an email seeking comments.
Experts told CNBC that while the scale of the protests does not pose a threat to the stability of India at present, crackdowns could broaden the unrest.

"If security forces keep taking heavy-handed approaches, this will create a more volatile environment that could make protestors angrier and galvanize even larger groups of marchers," Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council told CNBC.

He added that at present the scale of the protests was not significant enough to impact "capital flow and investor behavior" but warned that "heavy-handed tactics that generate violence and volatility" by the state could change it.

The United Nations Human Rights Office on Saturday raised concerns over mass detentions and called on Indian authorities "to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled."

On Sunday, India's Ministry of External Affairs responded to the UNHR's comments, calling them "unwarranted" and claiming they constituted an "unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of India."

The crackdown during the latest protest has been "significant and massive" compared to earlier reactions to farmers' protests or uniform civil code protests, Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at Teneo, told CNBC. He added that there is a higher chance that the broad-based retaliation to the police crackdown could lead to more demonstrations.

The CJP had first called for a nationwide protest on Oct. 2, seeking the removal of the election chief after an investigative report by the Indian Express showed discrepancies in the functioning of the Election Commission and reports of deletion of millions of voters.

On Sept. 26, following reports of the voter deletion, the Election Commission of India launched a special drive across India to enroll voters who have been left out of the rolls. It has downplayed discrepancies as highlighted in the Indian Express report and maintains it is "committed to ensuring that no eligible voter is left out of the voter list."

However, Modi's ruling party, the Bharatiya Janata Party, has defended the Election Commission and said the deletions were made on account of 28 million people who died, 68 million who relocated, 10 million with duplicate entries and 30 million absent or non-traceable voters.

The sweeping revisions of the electoral roll have raised serious constitutional and legal questions, Milan Vaishnav, director and senior fellow of the South Asia Program at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told CNBC.
The core demand of the movement is for Kumar to resign and for the commission to "seriously modify the so-called 'Special Intensive Revision' of the electoral rolls," he said.

articles.title: Feverish after a vaccine? The reason could be your gut microbiome

paras.en: Vaccines pack a punch: The shots save lives, but they can also often cause minor side effects such as muscle soreness, fatigue and fever. Researchers have long wondered why some people develop these reactions while others seem to skate by unaffected. The reason, it turns out, may have to do with the bacteria in our guts.

In a new study published in Science on Thursday, researchers collected stool samples from more than 170 people before and after a second or third dose of a COVID vaccine. They found that people who experienced fever after the shot tended to share similar microbiome traits.

Specifically, people with worse fever tended to have more of a protein called flagellin in their systems than those with little to no fever. Flagellin makes up the tail-like structures, or flagella, that bacteria use to move—suggesting that the fever-associated microbes had greater “motility,” or ability to move around, explains Ruth Ley, the study’s senior author and director of the department of microbiome science at the Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen in Germany. The participants with high-fever symptoms also tended to have greater gut inflammation than their peers.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

To investigate why, exactly, flagellin might influence fever, the researchers conducted a follow-up experiment in genetically engineered mice. They found that animals exposed to the fever-associated human bacteria showed a response equivalent to a fever in humans. This was particularly the case in those that could sense flagellin. Mice without flagellin receptors were less affected—indicating a direct link between flagellin and an immune system response.

On top of that, the levels of humans’ fever correlated with those of the equivalent reaction in mice, Ley says. “The worse the fever in the people, the more the temperature dropped in the mice,” she says. (Mice typically experience hypothermia as part of their immune response, which serves a similar function as a fever in humans.)

It’s still unclear why some people could have higher levels of flagellin in their guts than others. It may have something to do with diet: self-reported vegetarians tended to have lower flagellin levels, according to the study. But more research is needed to tease that out.

“It would make sense that, if you could tamp down the motility of the bacteria, we would predict that you wouldn’t react as strongly in terms of the fever,” Ley says. “But that’s all very much future research.”
Eventually, Ley hopes, the results could help fight this side effect of vaccines and, by extension, encourage higher vaccination rates.

articles.title: One doctor’s fight to make IUD placement better

paras.en: Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.

Intrauterine devices, more commonly known as IUDs, are some of the most effective forms of birth control options available. These small, T-shaped devices are placed directly into the uterus by way of the cervix, where they’re more than 99 percent effective at preventing pregnancy for years at a time. And copper IUDs, which rely on copper ions instead of hormones to limit sperm movement and egg fertilization, are also more than 99 percent effective as emergency contraception if placed within five days of unprotected sex.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But while IUDs are a set-it-and-forget-it solution, they do require a visit to the doctor for placement and eventual removal—and that process can be uncomfortable or even quite painful. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention now recommends that doctors counsel patients on pain medication options before an IUD insertion, but there’s not a lot of data out there about effective treatments. Options offered can include local anesthetic creams or injections directly to the cervix, conscious sedation or even full anesthesia—but there’s no real consensus on which intervention to use or how helpful some of them might be.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Today’s guest is the author of a recent study on a new method for mitigating the potential pain of IUD insertion. Helena Kopp Kallner is a professor at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden and senior consultant in obstetrics and gynecology at the Danderyd Hospital.
Thank you so much for coming on to chat with us today.
Helena Kopp Kallner: Thank you for having me.

Feltman: So you recently published a study on IUD insertion, but before we get into the research itself, I would love to give our listeners a little bit of context about IUDs. So could you tell us a little bit about what makes them such a great birth control option, but also what, you know, the potential downsides are that might keep some patients from getting them?

Kopp Kallner: So the very big upside with intrauterine contraception or IUDs is that they are user independent. So that means that you don’t have to think about taking something daily, weekly, monthly, or every three months. So it’s a type of fit-and-forget contraception, as we call it. That means that you have it placed, and then you don’t have to think about it. And, for some IUDs now, you can actually use them for up to eight or 10 years.

They’re also very, very effective, so perfect for young and highly fertile women who don’t wanna become pregnant just now. And for the hormonal IUDs, there’s also an upside with, like, reduction in menstrual flow, so you don’t bleed so much, and also reduction in menstrual pain. So those are the major upsides. But then the downside is that they can be painful to have fitted.
Feltman: Hmm. So tell me about, uh, how your new study came about?

Kopp Kallner: Well, actually, this has been quite a long process, as it usually is with clinical trials. But this was actually an idea that I had myself as I was fitting a lot of IUDs for very young women because I see a lot of very young women in my clinic with a lot of menstrual pain, and they are autistic, and they have lots of different issues. And I was just thinking that I needed to find something simple, so just like, “Okay, why don’t I just, like, inject some, local anesthetic through this, like, very, very thin catheter?” And then I was like, “Okay, now I have to do a study,” because I, I felt it worked. But then we started using a lower concentration of the same substance that we have been using now, and we did the pilot trial with around 80 patients. And then we got, like, near significance, and it was so annoying. And then we planned a larger study, so that’s what we have done now, and then we used a higher concentration of the local anesthetic. And it turned out that it, it works.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Feltman: So, prior to you trying this method, what pain relief and mitigation options were available to people getting IUDs inserted?

Kopp Kallner: I think the most common method still worldwide is just the use of anti-inflammatory drugs like ibuprofen and paracetamol that you take before the IUD insertion, although there are so many trials that have shown that this is not effective.

It works fine for pain after the placement or insertion, but not prophylactically. I think the second most common method is probably to use what we call a paracervical block. So that’s an injection with local anesthetic into the tissue with a needle, which is given on both sides of the cervix and then numbs the cervix and the uterus. But it has also been shown in studies that that method in itself is painful. So usually gynecologists and midwives are a bit reluctant to use that method because they feel that in a lot of patients you actually cause more pain with what’s supposed to cure the pain than what actually causes the pain. We only use it for those who really feel they need it or where we really feel like this is going to be painful.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Feltman: Right. Well, and, it’s occurring to me, I’m, unfortunately intimately familiar with why IUD insertion is painful. But, for people listening who have never had an IUD, could you walk us through what the process of insertion actually is, and, and why there is so much opportunity for discomfort and even pain?

Kopp Kallner: Well, I mean, the highest scientific standard of insertion of an IUD is to use, first of all, you use a speculum. That speculum, it visualizes the cervix because the IUD has to be inserted through the cervix into the uterus. So you visualize the cervix, and in some places you also clean the cervix. We don’t do that much in Europe, but in the U.S. it’s usually done, with an antiseptic. And then because the uterus is actually a curved organ, and you’re going to insert something straight into a curved organ, so you have to straighten it out. And, I think a lot of people have a lot of fear of the straightening process because usually that’s done with a so-called tenaculum. And the tenaculum is a very evil-looking kind of instrument with two claws that you, sort of, put onto the cervix. And for some women they don’t feel a thing. It’s not painful. And for others, this is very painful.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And then after that, usually, you use a so-called sound, which is also a, kind of, a straight instrument, and you use that to measure the length of the cervix and the uterus so that you are sure that you put the IUD up into, like, the bottom of the uterus. And that can also be painful. So you put the sound into the uterus, and then after that you do the IUD insertion.

And the IUD insertion has basically three painful parts of it. First of all is when you put the IUD insertion tube through what’s called the inner os. That’s the upper part of the cervix, and that is a very pain-sensitive part of the uterus.

And then, uh, you release the arms of the IUD. So that means that the arms, they’re folded in into the insertion tube, and then when you release the arms, that can also be painful because the IUD suddenly becomes bigger, so it sort of distends the uterine cavity a bit. And that can also be painful.

And then there is the final part of it, and that is when you actually push those arms that you’ve just distended, you push them up into the top of the uterus. Now, all of this, it sounds like it takes a lot of time because I’m, I’m speaking slow. But this is a really fast process. So all in all, from the very start to the very finish, if you have a good provider, this is going to take, like, less than a minute total. But it can be a very painful minute.

Feltman: Right. And it, it seems like for a procedure that’s so common and that potentially causes so much discomfort and frightens people, there aren’t many options, certainly not options that are easy and worthwhile for providers to implement to deal with that pain. Why do you think there’s that gap?

Kopp Kallner: So first of all, I think that the, the pain has largely been ignored because it’s a very short-lasting pain in most instances. And secondly, it’s only until the few last years that we have really been starting to insert a lot of IUDs in women who have not had children before.

And we know that women who have had children, especially who have given birth vaginally, that they have less pain than those who never have. And IUDs have traditionally been used for women who have completed their family. But now we inserted a lot of them in the very young for the obvious reasons that I stated in the beginning, that it’s a very effective method and long-lasting, so it’s very suitable for young women.

And that, of course, has also brought this pain issue more to the attention of providers and women. So I think that there has been a lack of research, and recently there have been a lot of trials investigating different methods for pain relief with IUD insertions, but they have either been found ineffective or painful in themselves.

And there are a lot of methods out there used, and people tell me, like, “No, but you should have been doing this, and you should have been doing that. And I do this, and that works fine for me.” And I’m like, “Yes, but have you done the actual study? How do you know that it actually works? Perhaps it’s just, like, placebo that you’re offering to patients.” And I think women deserve more. Women deserve a method that has actually been proven to be effective in a study so that they know that they’re just not being offered placebo. And if you think that your method is so great then do the study. Show the women that it is effective. That is what I have been doing, and I’m actually very proud of that.

People are so used to it being brushed aside that to some extent I think a provider offering anything goes such a long way into making a patient at least feel calmer. But to your point, how much better to have something that’s been empirically proven to actually help you.

Kopp Kallner: That is definitely correct. So this is a very, very thin, plastic catheter. And of course, maybe I should have looked up what it is in inches, but it’s 1.3 millimeters wide. So, it’s a very tiny catheter.

And this little catheter is then attached to a syringe with the 10 milliliters of the mepivacaine then, which is the local anesthetic that we use. And so it just like, it slips into the uterus very nicely actually.

And what happens then is that this fluid, it just, slowly runs out of the cervix, and it forms like a little puddle inside the vagina, and it sort of, like, drenches the cervix in this local anesthetic fluid. And then we apply the tenaculum to that part of the cervix that has been in the puddle, so to speak.

So perhaps it actually numbs the cervix as well. But that, we haven’t really studied so much. We got, in the pilot trial that I spoke about with the lower concentration of the mepivacaine, there we saw that the absolutely most painful part of the whole procedure was the actual placement of the IUD.

And then we told them, like, “Okay, now you need to score,” and they scored. And it was like, “Now you need to score,” and they scored. So it was, like, an immediate pain assessment. So it’s not like something, like, “Oh, 10 minutes after I thought like, you know, I experienced this kinda thing I remember.” So it’s a very exact kind of pain assessment. So it’s from the absolute worst pain imaginable—sort of like, what if somebody were to saw off your legs with a really rusty saw and you had no anesthesia—to, like, you wake up in the morning, you’re completely pain free, the sun is shining. You score in between those.

But if patients start asking for it, like, “Oh, I want this evidence-based pain relief,” and the doctor goes like, “Oh, what is that?” And they’re like, “Oh, do I have to educate you?” So I think that when we educate women, when we educate our patients, that’s when change happens more rapidly.

articles.title: Could Tutankhamun's tomb hold clues to a mysterious Egyptian queen?

paras.en: A growing body of research is generating renewed interest in potential hidden spaces beyond the decorated walls of Tutankhamun’s burial chamber in Egypt.

Some researchers have raised the possibility that these concealed chambers—if they exist—could contain the burial place of Nefertiti, Tutankhamun’s stepmother and mother-in-law. Nefertiti was made famous by a remarkable painted bust of her head found in Tell-el Amarna, Egypt, in 1912.

The hypothesis about hidden rooms was first proposed more than a decade ago. A key advocate of the idea, archaeologist Nicholas Reeves, mentions clues that he believes may point to Nefertiti’s burial being nearby. These include “hidden” hieroglyphics that were painted over on the north wall of Tutankhamun’s tomb.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

A team has now published a review of archaeological and geophysical investigations at Tutankhamun’s burial chamber (also known as KV62), including results from a survey carried out between 2023 and 2024.

Lead researcher Mamdouh Eldamaty told Nature that the results were suggestive of concealed structures beyond KV62. A decision on whether to carefully drill through the north wall and deploy miniature cameras could be made in coming months. However, other experts are cautious about the findings.

There is a delicate balance between speculation, hypothesis testing, and discovery. Some of the greatest scientific and archaeological breakthroughs have come from researchers willing to challenge paradigms and pursue ideas drawn from vague and improbable historical clues.

However, limited evidence combined with great expectations can encourage conclusions that run ahead of the data. The possibility of hidden chambers beyond the tomb of Tutankhamun sits precisely at this intersection.

Yet the distinction between evidence for unexplored spaces and evidence for the burial of Nefertiti remains substantial. The challenge is not to decide what we hope to find, but to evaluate objectively what the available evidence does, and does not, support.
The media readily gravitates toward the most spectacular conclusions. The search for Cleopatra’s tomb at Taposiris Magna provides a cautionary example.

Previously looted tombs, artifacts, and even the renewed investigation of a subterranean hydraulic tunnel were frequently presented as indications that the discovery of Cleopatra’s tomb was imminent. Yet the existence of an aqueduct consistent with Hellenistic (Greek-influenced) urban infrastructure does not constitute evidence for a royal burial.

A more measured approach can be seen in the work of Greek archaeologist Calliope Papakosta in Alexandria, Egypt. During a visit to her excavations, she showed me evidence suggesting that Alexander the Great’s tomb might lie nearby. The most compelling object was a marble statue of a young warrior that she argued, and I agree, may depict Alexander.
The style was consistent with the school of Lysippus, Alexander’s court sculptor. Unfortunately, the sculpture had been discarded within a Roman fill layer and thus removed from its original context.

Papakosta recognized both the promise and limitations of the evidence. While hopeful that her work might illuminate the fate of Alexander’s tomb, she consistently framed her discoveries within the bounds of what the data demonstrated.

The debate surrounding Tutankhamun’s tomb raises similar issues. The burial site is unusually small for one hosting a pharaoh, and Nicholas Reeves has argued that it represents only the outer portion of a larger Amarna-period (roughly 1350–1325 BC) royal burial complex.
The abnormality of the tomb is widely accepted and it has been presumed to be a small private tomb that was hastily adapted for the king because of his death at a young age.

A suggestion of door seams in the decorated north wall of the burial chamber stimulated the extended tomb complex theory, but damaging the wall to probe it would be out of the question. Progress would therefore depend upon geophysics providing a means to peer through the wall without damaging it.

The first investigations employed relatively low-frequency Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR), principally in the 400-900 megahertz (MHz) range. Such frequencies provide greater penetration into the surrounding limestone than higher-frequency radar. But this comes at the expense of spatial resolution. Later investigations expanded this range and included frequencies as high as 3 gigahertz (GHz).

My own inclination would have been to place particular emphasis on the highest-frequency radar antennae (the parts of the GPR system that transmit and receive electromagnetic pulses) because resolving whether the north wall contains evidence of a door seam is an important first step to answering other key questions.
High-frequency systems offer less penetration but are generally better suited to detecting subtle structural discontinuities immediately behind the wall surface.

More recent investigations added microgravity surveys made from above the theorized complex. These measure minute variations in the Earth’s gravitational field caused by differences in density below ground. Higher-frequency GPR has also now been added to the team’s toolkit.
This was a sensible evolution of the research strategy. The problem was, to protect the wall paintings, the GPR antennae could not be placed directly against the decorated surfaces.

The resulting air gap weakened coupling between the antenna and the wall, reducing signal quality and complicating interpretation. For GPR, the farther the antenna is from the surface, the more difficult it becomes to resolve subtle architectural features.

Microgravity surveys do not suffer from this limitation. They are capable of identifying anomalies within the limestone below the sensor. The challenge facing both types of investigation is that they have not produced unambiguous evidence for a large open chamber immediately beyond the wall.

To account for this, proponents of the hidden chamber hypothesis have suggested that any passageways may have been deliberately backfilled with rubble, obscuring the void signatures that investigators originally expected to detect. This is plausible and merits further testing, but it remains an interpretation, not fact.
Some investigators have argued that the currently available geophysical evidence does not demonstrate the presence of hidden chambers.

This has led to the next logical step in the scientific process: direct testing. The current proposal to drill a small borehole and deploy miniature cameras into one of the identified anomalies has the potential to move the discussion from inference to observation.
Whatever the outcome, the investigations undertaken by Eldamaty and colleagues represent the most comprehensive scientific assessment of the question to date.
Currently, the hidden chamber theory remains exactly what a good scientific hypothesis should be: intriguing, testable, and worthy of investigation. What it is not, at least yet, is a discovery.

articles.title: The world’s loudest bird could drown out a rock concert
articles.author: Elie Dolgin

paras.en: The bare-throated bellbird is loud. Very, very loud.

The explosive, metallic mating call of the snow-white male — a stout bird with a broad bill and distinctive blue-green throat patch — can top 130 decibels, louder than a jackhammer or a front-row seat at a Counting Crows concert.

That makes this South American forest dweller a contender for the title of world’s loudest bird. And now researchers think they know how it and other avian loudmouths produce such eardrum-rattling vocalizations.

Bigger bodies and, especially, wider beaks help these feathered screamers belt it out, behavioral ecologists João Menezes and Jeff Podos of the University of Massachusetts Amherst report September 29 in Evolution.

But what pushed some birds to evolve such volume in the first place remains a mystery. The researchers looked at mating behavior, habitat density and flight ability, but found no explanation that consistently held across species. “We weren’t able to find an overarching pattern that applies to birds in general,” Menezes says.

The quest to understand these sonic extremes dates back to 2019. That is when Podos and a colleague crowned the white bellbird (Procnias albus), an Amazonian cousin of the bare-throated bellbird (P. nudicollis), as a record-setting vocal powerhouse. Its 125-decibel calls were the loudest bird calls ever measured at the time.
Beyond the attention-grabbing number, the finding raised a broader question: What makes some birds so extraordinarily loud?

The honk of a Canada goose, for example, can reach chainsaw volume (100 decibels), while the chatter of a starling rarely rises above a dishwasher-level hum (70 decibels) — and ornithologists have surprisingly little understanding of why. Although scientists have spent decades cataloging the timing and frequency of birdsong, hoping to decode what birds are saying, the sheer loudness of bird voices has gone largely unexplored.

To get a read on the racket, Podos lugged a high-grade sound meter, the kind used to monitor noise levels in industrial workplaces, and a laser rangefinder into the woods, swamps and open fields around his home in western Massachusetts. He measured the calls of whatever birds he could find — warblers, sparrows, robins and more.

After logging a few dozen species, he enlisted Menezes, a then-grad student who at the time had recently joined his lab, to help turn the collection into a broader evolutionary analysis. Menezes measured bird vocalizations across his home country of Brazil, from the Atlantic Forest near São Paulo to the mountains surrounding Rio de Janeiro and beyond. He captured everything from the soft chirps of the dusky-throated hermit hummingbird to the piercing yelps of the red-legged seriema, a shaggy type of grassland bird.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: All told, he and Podos compiled vocal volume data on 123 species, creating what they say is the largest such dataset to date.

The heftier the bird, the louder its call tended to be, and the same went for birds with broader beaks — a connection between anatomy and acoustic performance that biophysicist Gabriel Mindlin from the University of Buenos Aires in Argentina finds “sensible and plausible.”

“Larger birds have the potential to generate greater respiratory pressures and flows, while morphological features such as beak opening can affect how efficiently acoustic energy radiates,” says Mindlin, who studies birdsong but was not involved in the work.
Why evolution cranked up the volume on these avian megaphones, though, is a puzzle that remains, for now, unhatched.

articles.title: ‘A Mother’s Brain’ explores the neuroscience of motherhood
articles.author: Laura Sanders

paras.en: When it comes to new motherhood, the baby typically takes center stage, garnering most of people’s attention. But in a refreshing twist, neuroscientist Susana Carmona shifts the spotlight to the mom. In the opening pages of A Mother’s Brain, Carmona cheerfully tells us, “here, we’ll hardly discuss babies at all.” Mothers are her protagonists.

What follows is a captivating, passionate and well-grounded journey through the fascinating process of “matrescence.” A word coined to echo “adolescence,” another time of seismic changes, matrescence includes the intense reorganization a woman’s brain undergoes as she becomes a mom. So far, early studies have revealed a sculpting of brain circuits (and Carmona is quick to point out that less can be more), heightened social instincts and perhaps even a boost of resilience during old age.

This mom found the book to be a treasure trove of motherly delights. Scientific concepts are woven with social and cultural strands, from the poignant to the weird to the profound. Certain passages in the book allowed me the pleasure of relistening to the song “The Mother” by Brandi Carlile, in which she sings, “Welcome to the end of being alone inside your mind.” A Mother’s Brain also kindly pointed me to the viral video, “Mother Rat Saves Baby from Snake.”

As one of the foremost scientists studying matrescence, Carmona is an authoritative guide through the latest research, of which there is a dismayingly small amount. Still, the book covers scientific ground including hormones, evolution and brain networks. History, social constructs and the pressures of modern life come into the story, too.

If you prefer a light read, Carmona will occasionally warn you when a section is scientifically dense. Then she will invite you along anyway. “But if you do like hormones — well, we’re going to have fun,” Carmona writes at the beginning of a chapter. And it was fun. I was shocked to learn, for instance, just how massive the hormonal upheaval during pregnancy is. The amount of estrogen that floods a woman’s body, including her brain, during the 40 weeks of pregnancy is more than that of the amount that would otherwise accumulate over her entire fertile life, which lasts 35 years on average.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Along the way, Carmona thoughtfully addresses scientific puzzlers such as this: Mothers often report feeling less mentally sharp, yet laboratory studies show almost no neurological decline. Attributed to “mommy brain” or “momnesia,” mental slips might be due to a lack of sleep, or a shifting of attention, or even just an expectation.

This pervasive, negative stereotype of “mommy brain” can then build on itself, getting stronger as women buy into the incorrect idea that motherhood leaves them dumber. If a woman expects her memory to get worse, she’ll see signs of it in even normal mistakes. “I have watched brilliant women grow so insecure about their intelligence on becoming mothers that they abandon the projects that were once vital to them,” Carmona writes. Assumptions about their diminished brainpower can lead women to pull back from valuable parts of their lives. “It matters — a lot — how we talk to ourselves about these things.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: As a mother herself, Carmona brings her experiences into the narrative. It couldn’t be any other way. “Motherhood is lived,” she writes. “It happens in your gut, your identity, your core.”

At its heart, this book is a love letter to moms, who have been invisible to the scientific gaze for too long. It’s time to write a new tale of matrescence, Carmona argues. “A story that recognizes mothers as the essence of the human species, the carriers of knowledge about how we create bonds — and, through them, society and culture.”
By putting the intense and wild changes of motherhood into words, Carmona offers us a powerful and necessary story.

articles.title: An extinct crocodilian was found among rocks that built the Great Sphinx
articles.author: Jake Buehler

paras.en: The Great Sphinx of Giza isn’t the only ancient, stony visage in the area missing its nose.

A fossil crocodilian discovered in the same 45-million-year-old limestone that ancient Egyptians used to build the Sphinx is also missing the tip of its snout. But the broken specimen is intact enough to be reclassified as a new branch of the gavial family tree, which may help uncover these mysterious animals’ evolutionary history, researchers report October 7 in Royal Society Open Science.

Most living crocodilians are in either the crocodile or alligator families. But there are also two species of gavial living in tropical Asia. These are huge, critically endangered, fish-eating crocodilians with long, slender snouts full of needlelike teeth. Fossils of extinct gavials have been found around the world. In 1927, German researchers reported a gavial skull fossil collected from hills near Cairo. The fossil was identified as an extinct species of Tomistoma, a genus found today only as a single species in Southeast Asia.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But more recent evolutionary studies including this fossil suggested this classification didn’t fit. In 2023, while working on a doctoral degree at University College London, paleontologist Paul Burke went to Germany to study the fossil in detail. Burke and his colleagues made careful measurements of the skull, using 3-D X-ray methods to measure the insides of the brain and nasal cavities.

“As we’ve advanced in the last 100 years, we’ve got so many new methodologies we could implement to figure out what kind of species this fossil is,” says Burke, currently at the Sweden Museum of Natural History in Stockholm.

The team compared the measurements to those taken of living and fossil gavials and found that this purported Egyptian Tomistoma was actually an undescribed gavial genus. The researchers named it Herugavialis cairensis, referencing the Egyptian god Heru (or Horus), who has been associated with the Great Sphinx. Coincidentally, the Herugavialis skull is missing the end of its snout — something it shares with the noseless statue.
“So many species are found from the same [geologic] formation,” Burke says, including fish, sharks and mammals. “But this is the first one with the name associated with the Sphinx.”

Today, gavials are only found in freshwater environments. But tens of millions of years ago, the reptiles also inhabited nearshore saltwater environments. Herugavialis appears to have been a coastal predator back when the ancient Tethys Ocean covered northern Egypt.

Khalafallah Salih, a paleontologist at Al Neelain University in Khartoum, Sudan, says the finding supports the idea that the evolution of gavials and their relatives in Africa was much more complex than researchers thought. Herugavialis doesn’t appear closely related to other known gavial-type crocodilians in Africa or the Mediterranean, he says. It appears to have branched off from the lineage early in its evolution.
Burke notes that gavials barely breach the public consciousness compared to alligators and crocodiles.
“They’re still alive today and they’re endangered,” he says. “So, we should know about them and their long history.”

articles.title: The eye has a hidden cleanup system scientists never knew existed

paras.en: The eye has a hidden cleanup system scientists never knew existed
Scientists have uncovered a hidden waste removal system in the eye that could transform how we understand and treat blinding diseases.

- Scientists have discovered a hidden cleanup system at the back of the eye that drains fluid and waste through a previously unknown pathway. The surprising finding, demonstrated in mice, could open the door to new treatments for glaucoma, macular degeneration, and other causes of blindness.

Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown cleanup system at the back of the eye, revealing a hidden route that allows fluid and waste to escape into the body's lymphatic system. The discovery challenges long-standing assumptions about how the eye functions and could eventually lead to new approaches for treating serious conditions that cause blindness.

Glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, and several other major causes of permanent vision loss are associated with the accumulation of fluid, metabolic waste, and inflammatory material in the back of the eye. Until now, researchers have struggled to explain exactly how this sensitive region removes unwanted substances.

A team from the University of British Columbia (UBC) and the University of Toronto has identified a previously unrecognized drainage route called the posterior ocular lymphatic outflow, or POLO pathway. The system appears to carry fluid and waste away from the back of the eye and into the lymphatic network, which helps the body maintain fluid balance, remove waste, and support immune defenses.
The finding, demonstrated in mice, offers scientists a new way to investigate how the eye protects its delicate tissues and what happens when waste removal is disrupted.

"The retina is one of the most metabolically active parts of the body, constantly generating byproducts that need to be cleared," said Dr. Neeru Gupta, professor and head of UBC's department of ophthalmology and visual sciences. "This discovery helps explain how the eye flushes this waste and promises to transform how we think about and treat a range of eye conditions."
A Hidden Eye Drainage System Could Open New Paths to Treatment

The retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye, requires substantial energy to convert incoming light into signals the brain can interpret. This constant activity produces metabolic byproducts that must be removed to keep the surrounding tissues functioning properly.

When fluid and waste accumulate, they can contribute to conditions that damage the eye. Glaucoma, macular degeneration, and other retinal disorders are associated with changes in fluid regulation, cellular waste buildup, tissue stress, and inflammation.
Age-related macular degeneration alone affects approximately 2.5 million Canadians, highlighting the potential importance of understanding the processes that keep the retina healthy.

The newly identified POLO pathway suggests that the back of the eye has a natural mechanism for moving unwanted material out of this vulnerable region. If scientists can determine how that mechanism works and whether it can be strengthened, it could provide a new target for therapies designed to protect vision.

"This gives us a whole new framework for understanding these diseases and a potential target for therapeutics," said Dr. Gupta. "The question now is: How can we enhance or exploit this cleanup system to treat or even prevent disease."
A Discovery That Challenges More Than a Century of Assumptions
For over 100 years, scientists generally believed that the eye lacked the lymphatic drainage systems found in nearly every other organ.

The lymphatic system consists of vessels and tissues that collect excess fluid, transport certain waste products, and help coordinate immune responses. It works alongside the blood circulatory system to maintain healthy conditions throughout the body.
The idea that the eye was largely separate from this network began to change in 2009, when Dr. Gupta and Dr. Yeni Yücel identified a lymphatic-related drainage route in the front of the eye.
They named it the "uveolymphatic" pathway, providing evidence that the eye had previously unrecognized connections to the body's fluid clearance mechanisms.
Dr. Yücel, a professor and director of ophthalmic pathology at the University of Toronto, continued investigating the possibility that similar pathways might exist elsewhere in the eye.

Despite that earlier discovery, the back of the eye remained relatively unexplored. This was a particularly important gap because the retina and surrounding tissues are affected by some of the most serious diseases responsible for permanent vision loss.

"The retina is responsible for vision and it's also where many of the most serious vision-loss diseases occur," said Dr. Yücel. "Understanding how this part of the eye maintains a balanced environment and flow of materials is critical."
Scientists Trace a Secret Cleanup Route Behind the Retina

To investigate how fluid leaves the back of the eye, the researchers combined several advanced imaging methods in mice, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), near-infrared fluorescence imaging, and microscopic examination.

They placed fluorescent tracer molecules into a narrow space at the rear of the eye. Because these molecules could be detected as they moved, the scientists were able to follow the fluid's path and determine where it traveled.

The results revealed tiny lymphatic vessels in the choroid, a thin, blood vessel-rich layer located beneath the retina. The choroid plays an important role in nourishing the outer retina, but lymphatic vessels had not previously been established in this region.

The team observed fluid moving from the back of the eye into the surrounding orbital tissues, which occupy the space around the eyeball. Within minutes, the tracers reached nearby lymph nodes, connecting the eye's newly identified drainage route to the body's broader lymphatic system.
This provided evidence that fluid from the back of the eye could enter an active drainage pathway rather than remaining confined within the eye.

"Because lymphatic vessels in the choroid were thought not to exist, the team used multiple techniques to demonstrate both their presence and function," added Dr. Yücel, a pathologist-scientist at St. Michael's Hospital. "We were surprised to see such a direct route for fluid to leave the eye and connect with the lymphatic system. It suggests the back of the eye has an active clearance pathway, which could play an important role in removing fluid, proteins and inflammatory material that build up in disease."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Could the Eye's Cleanup System Help Prevent Blindness?
Although the discovery offers a new explanation for how fluid and waste may leave the back of the eye, important questions remain.

The experiments were conducted in mice, and further studies are necessary to establish how the POLO pathway functions in humans. Researchers also need to determine whether changes in this drainage system contribute to eye disease and whether its activity can be safely modified.
If those questions can be answered, the pathway could eventually offer several possibilities for treatment.

One approach might involve developing therapies that improve fluid clearance, potentially reducing the buildup of substances associated with inflammation and tissue damage. Another possibility is using knowledge of this drainage route to improve how medications are delivered to structures deep within the eye.
Understanding the system may also help researchers investigate how pressure, inflammation, and fluid movement interact in conditions such as glaucoma and age-related macular degeneration.

These applications remain potential future developments rather than established treatments. Nevertheless, the discovery gives scientists a new anatomical pathway to study and a possible explanation for processes that have remained poorly understood for decades.

"This is a foundational discovery that shows the eye is not as closed a system as we previously thought," said Dr. Gupta. "It gives us a new map, a new mechanism and a new set of questions to explore."
The findings were published in the scientific journal Translational Vision Science & Technology.
