articles.title: Diagnosing GM Super Cruise Systems
articles.author: Andrew Markel

paras.en: Super Cruise is GM’s hands-free driver-assistance system, offered on certain 2019-205 GM vehicles. Feature-wise, it combines adaptive cruise control, automatic braking, lane centering, driver monitoring, GPS and high-definition map data.

In the shop, diagnosis starts by separating a component fault or configuration problem from a normal system inhibit. A missing condition or failure in any of the above-mentioned areas can prevent engagement.

On an approved mapped road, Super Cruise uses Adaptive Cruise Control to manage speed and following distance while the lane-control system commands electric power steering to center the vehicle. The forward camera supplies lane information, and Adaptive Cruise Control sensing hardware tracks traffic ahead. The engine and electronic brake control modules carry out acceleration and braking requests. Because these modules exchange network data, a voltage, communication or configuration fault outside the camera can disable the system.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Super Cruise also compares GPS position with its map database. GM service information identifies the K179 Automated Driving Mapping Module and a LiDAR-scanned map database. Map and GPS-enhancement updates are downloaded through the vehicle’s OnStar Wi-Fi connection. The K73 telematics module supplies GPS and connectivity functions. If the vehicle cannot establish its location or does not have usable road data, Super Cruise cannot confirm that the road is eligible.

Before condemning hardware, verify the enabling conditions. Adaptive Cruise Control must be on, the Forward Collision System set to Alert and Brake, the road approved in the map database, lane markings visible, sensors unobstructed and the driver attentive. Teen Driver mode cannot be active. An OnStar plan and accepted terms may also be required. Requirements vary by model year and RPO, so identify the vehicle configuration before testing.

The secondary DIC message is often more useful than the general statement that Super Cruise is unavailable. “No Road Information” may indicate an ineligible road, an interchange, reconstruction, missing map data or lost GPS. The message “Sensors Can’t Find Lane Lines” can result from weak markings, glare or precipitation. “Sensor Blocked” points toward contamination. Other normal inhibits include an exit lane, a sharp curve, failure to center the vehicle or excessive speed. The referenced GM application lists 85 MPH, although limits are calibration-dependent.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Could Not Recognize Face,” “Can’t See Face Clearly,” “Driver Attention Assist Unavailable,” momentary engagement followed by a takeover warning, and unexplained disengagement can originate in the monitoring system. Check for glare, a dirty lens, obstructions, steering-column position, a hand covering the infrared emitters, a loose B292 camera in the upper shroud, wiring damage or failed emitters. These complaints may occur without a DTC.

First, record the exact messages the customer received, along with road and location, weather, lighting, speed, engagement time and repeatability. Ask them about recent windshield, collision, steering, alignment, suspension, camera, radar or module work. Verify the OnStar account and terms when applicable, plus Wi-Fi and map-update status.

Next, perform GM’s vehicle diagnostic system check. Confirm battery state of charge, 9-16 V operating voltage where specified, clean and tight cables and grounds, intact fuses, seated connectors, correct power modes and the absence of interfering aftermarket equipment. Inspect lenses, radar areas and the steering-column camera before connecting the scan tool.

Run a full vehicle DTC scan and document every non-communicating module, DTC, symptom byte and current or history status. Do not erase evidence first. Diagnose voltage, internal-module, communication, power-mode and serial-data authentication faults before the Super Cruise symptom. Check applicable bulletins and calibrations. On covered 2021-2024 vehicles, intermittent startup U1624 in K124 may be a false loss-of-Ethernet fault caused by K73 telematics software; follow the bulletin and update K73. For other programmable modules, GM directs current software and a retest before replacement. Cruise data can retain the last eight disengagement reasons and the most recent engagement inhibit.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: For “No Road Information” without a related DTC, move the vehicle to an open-sky area and inspect the K73 telematics data, including Number of Satellites Tracked when available. A value that remains at zero, or an incorrect location during an OnStar blue-button check, supports a GPS or telematics fault on vehicles covered by the applicable bulletin. Separate that failure from temporary map, road or reception limits.

For low-light face-recognition complaints, verify all three infrared emitters on each side of the steering-wheel light bar. GDS2 can command them through K124 Image Processing Module 1 Processor 2 under Configuration Reset Functions and Driver Monitoring System Illumination Command. GM recommends a phone camera with a long-exposure function because infrared output may be difficult to see. If one side is dark, follow the VIN-specific circuit diagnostics.

Programming, setup and calibration requirements differ across the 2019-2025 range. Confirm RPO content and follow the exact SI procedure after related components are replaced or disturbed. Some 2022-2023 vehicles with RPO 07Z use an image-processing module only to complete CAN circuits. Installing a functional replacement can create a “Take Steering Wheel” message unless the published configuration procedure is followed.

Complete all required programming, setup and calibrations, then clear the codes only as directed. Road-test the vehicle safely on a known compatible route and reproduce the original conditions. Confirm that the enabling indicators appear, the original DIC message does not return, driver monitoring responds and no faults reset. A successful bay check does not prove the complaint is resolved by itself.

articles.title: Where Steering and Suspension Problems Come From
articles.author: TrakMotive

paras.en: Ever drive a vehicle that just doesn’t feel right anymore? Maybe it wanders down the highway. Maybe there’s a clunk every time you hit a pothole. Maybe the steering wheel isn’t centered, the tires are wearing unevenly, or it just doesn’t inspire the confidence it used to.

The truth is, steering and suspension problems rarely come from a single worn out part. Every control arm, ball joint, tie rod, sway bar link, and bushing work together as one connected system. When one connection starts to wear, it puts added stress on the rest of the system, and before long, that small problem becomes several bigger ones.
That system level approach is exactly how TrakMotive has positioned its Suspensia brand chassis program. Learn more about it in this video, sponsored by TrakMotive.

articles.title: How Scotty’s Automotive Delivers Dealer Level Diagnostics

From full-system scans and CAN bus diagnostics to Remote Expert programming, TPMS service and digital tire inspections, the team shows how the right tools help keep more work in-house. Discover how modern diagnostic technology can save technicians time, improve shop efficiency and help independent repair facilities deliver dealership-level capabilities to their customers.

articles.title: Schaeffler, Qorix Partner on Software-Defined Vehicle Platforms
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: Schaeffler and Qorix have entered into a strategic partnership to jointly develop, integrate and market software-based platform solutions. The companies will focus on future vehicle architectures and intelligent machines. Together, the companies aim to advance integrated hardware and software solutions for central vehicle computers and software-defined architectures.

The collaboration combines Schaeffler’s expertise in system integration and safety-critical driving and comfort functions with Qorix’s production-ready middleware technologies. It also incorporates Qorix’s integration expertise in central computing platforms and active involvement in the Eclipse S-CORE open-source ecosystem.

“With our platform and integration expertise, Schaeffler is laying the foundation for central software-defined vehicle architectures. Qorix complements this foundation with production-ready middleware and a strong open-source approach, enabling us to bring scalable solutions to market faster and more efficiently,” said Thomas Stierle, CEO E-Mobility at Schaeffler AG.
Schaeffler, Qorix Address New Vehicle Architecture Requirements

The shift from distributed electronic control unit architectures to central high-performance computing platforms presents the automotive industry with new requirements. The industry needs reliable middleware and software platforms that meet standards for scalability, security and production readiness.
Schaeffler contributes hardware platforms, cross-domain controller solutions and many years of experience in system integration.

Qorix complements these strengths with Qorix Performance, which provides deterministic communication and end-to-end management throughout the entire product life cycle. The technology also supports functional safety in accordance with ISO 26262.
Together, the partners aim to reduce integration efforts, shorten development times and accelerate the industrialization of software-defined vehicle architectures.
Open Source Provides Technological Foundation
Both companies participate in Eclipse S-CORE, an open-source software framework for software-defined vehicles.
Their involvement supports faster, more consistent development and reduces integration efforts. It also enables software reuse across vehicle generations and customer programs.

“With Schaeffler as a strategic partner, we are accelerating exactly what drives us: bringing production-ready, open-source-based software platforms to market faster. Qorix Performance combined with Schaeffler’s system integration and compute expertise creates a compelling offering for automotive manufacturers and Tier 1 suppliers that want to actively shape the transition to software-defined architectures,” said Markus Schupfner, CEO of Qorix.

articles.title: Goodyear Elects Joe Hinrichs Chairman of Board of Directors
articles.author: Jeff White

paras.en: Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. announced the election of Joe Hinrichs as chairman of its board of directors, effective Oct. 7, 2026. Hinrichs will also chair the board’s governance and executive committees. He joined the company’s board in 2023. Hinrichs succeeds Laurette Koellner, who will retire at the company’s 2027 annual meeting in accordance with Goodyear’s Corporate Governance Guidelines.
Goodyear Chairman Brings Automotive Leadership Experience

Hinrichs most recently served as president and chief executive officer of CSX Corp. Before joining CSX, he held numerous leadership roles at Ford Motor Co., including president of the Global Automotive Business. He also served as executive vice president and president of Global Operations. His other positions included executive vice president and president of the Americas and president of Asia Pacific and Africa. He also served as chairman and chief executive officer of Ford China and president and chief executive officer of Ford Canada.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Hinrichs holds a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering from the University of Dayton and an MBA from Harvard Business School.

Koellner previously held several leadership roles at The Boeing Co. She joined Goodyear’s board of directors in 2015 and became independent lead director in 2019. She became nonexecutive chairman of the board in 2024.

“I would like to recognize and thank Laurette for her leadership, dedication and unwavering commitment to Goodyear. On behalf of the Board, we are grateful for her many contributions throughout her more than a decade of service,” said Hinrichs. “I look forward to working alongside my fellow board members and the leadership team as we continue to innovate, strengthen our competitive position, create long-term value for our shareholders and build a stronger Goodyear.”

articles.title: Mishimoto Names Joe DeLorme Vice President of Product
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: Performance automotive aftermarket brand Mishimoto announced the appointment of Joe DeLorme as vice president of product.

In this role, DeLorme will lead product strategy, new product development, product management and portfolio optimization across Mishimoto’s growing portfolio of automotive performance products. He will be responsible for driving innovation, accelerating speed to market, and strengthening alignment between customer needs and business objectives.

DeLorme joins Mishimoto with more than 17 years of leadership experience spanning product management, sales and strategic planning. Throughout his career, he has successfully led cross-functional teams, launched category defining products and implemented processes that improve execution, profitability and customer satisfaction.

“I am excited to join Mishimoto and contribute to the company’s continued success,” said DeLorme. “Mishimoto has built a strong reputation for innovation and customer focus. I look forward to working alongside the talented team to expand our product offerings, enhance the customer experience and drive long-term growth.”

As vice president of product, DeLorme will focus on strengthening product development capabilities, improving portfolio performance and ensuring the company continues to deliver innovative solutions that meet the evolving needs of automotive enthusiasts around the world, the company said.

articles.title: Automotive Parts Services Group CEO Jeff Koviak on Multiplying Successes
articles.author: Mary DellaValle

paras.en: This episode of DriveTime features Jeff Koviak, CEO, Automotive Parts Services Group.

Koviak said he views industry consolidation as an inevitable evolution that can ultimately make the independent aftermarket stronger and more competitive. Rather than becoming “distracted by the noise,” he believes Automotive Parts Services Group members should remain focused on running their businesses and getting their parts through the supply chain and installed onto cars. Koviak sees consolidation creating stronger organizations through investment and greater efficiencies, helping the independent aftermarket compete more effectively with OEM service centers.

articles.title: Counter Culture: Understanding Torque Converter Shudder
articles.author: Counterman Staff

paras.en: In the latest episode of Counter Culture, Pat Burrow, technical director at International Lubricants, discusses the causes of torque converter shudder. He also explains the importance of transmission fluid and how friction modifiers can help technicians diagnose and address the problem.
Burrow Explains Causes of Torque Converter Shudder

Burrow explains that torque converter shudder often feels like driving over railroad tracks, with vibrations ranging from barely noticeable to severe. Although mechanical wear, solenoids and transmission programming can contribute, depleted fluid additives frequently play a significant role.
“Transmission fluid is probably the most complicated lubricant you have in your vehicle,” Burrow said.
Beyond lubrication, transmission fluid provides cooling, wear protection, hydraulic operation and smooth clutch engagement.

Burrow explains that modern automatic transmission fluids contain friction modifiers designed for specific applications. However, demanding driving conditions can accelerate additive depletion, sometimes causing shudder after just 20,000 to 30,000 miles.

Burrow emphasizes asking customers about vehicle mileage, driving conditions and specific applications before recommending a solution. Heavy loads, high temperatures and stop-and-go traffic can increase the likelihood of fluid-related problems.

Burrow also discusses how friction modifiers can serve as diagnostic tools. If a friction modifier reduces or eliminates shudder, technicians can identify fluid-related issues before pursuing mechanical repairs.
“If the shutter went away, boom, they knew instantly what the problem was. It was fluid,” Burrow said.
However, Burrow cautions that worn solenoids, valve bodies and other mechanical problems may require repairs that fluid additives cannot address.

articles.title: Self-driving, solar-powered cars that talk to each other? What vehicles might look like in 10 years.
articles.author: Skyler Ware

paras.en: Imagine you're road-tripping across the country 10 years from now. You spend a few minutes charging your electric vehicle and then set off — and your car's solar paint keeps it charged as you drive.

Your eyes are on the stunning scenery, taking in the vistas along Route 66 or the grandeur of the Rocky Mountains, or you're catching up on messages. Your hands barely touch the wheel, and your foot doesn't push a pedal. Your car communicates with others on the road, so there's no need to brake suddenly or swerve. That's because it knows a vehicle five cars up from you has done so, and all those in between are slowing at exactly the right pace to avoid dramatic changes in trajectory.

And when you park for the night, your car makes you money, selling the excess energy it's harvested from its paint back to the grid. Or maybe you don't feel like being in the driver's seat at all, so you hail a self-driving car and take a nap in the back seat in between adventures.

Some of that scenario may become a reality in the next 10 years, at least for those who are using the most cutting-edge cars on the market. Although there's some heavy speculation involved in that futuristic vision, vehicle manufacturers are already incorporating increasingly sophisticated automated driving technology into high-end personal vehicles, and self-driving taxis are coming to dozens of U.S. cities.

What's more, dramatic changes in range, cost and charging speed for electric vehicles (EVs) are arriving at a rapid pace. While some of these technologies may not wind up in personal cars, others are already taking to the roads.

Some car models within the next decade may interact with their surroundings in new ways, including by communicating with other cars to avoid collisions, drawing energy from natural sources, or letting drivers get paid for sending their cars' unused energy back to the grid.

If you're driving an EV, you might avoid the hassle of finding a charger when you're at work or running errands. In 2024, EV company Aptera unveiled a prototype car equipped with solar panels. Those panels — on the car's hood, roof, dashboard and hatch — allow the vehicle to travel about 40 miles (64 kilometers) per day on solar power. That's more than the average American drives per day. Aptera's vehicle can also travel up to 400 miles (640 km) on a standard electrical charge.

Some sunlight-powered cars might ditch the solar panels altogether in favor of a more integrated design. In 2024, Mercedes-Benz revealed it was researching a photovoltaic paint that could convert sunlight into energy for electric cars. In sunny cities such as Los Angeles, the company calculated, the paint could draw in enough energy to power the car for nearly 7,500 miles (12,000 km) per year. The tiny particles in the paint convert about 20% of the energy from sunlight into electricity, which is comparable to the efficiency of existing solar panels.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: You might even be able to sell some of the energy stored in your car's battery back to the grid. EV owners could charge during the day or late at night, when the demand for electricity is lower and pay lower rates for electricity. Then, in the evenings when the electrical grid is under more strain and the price of electricity is higher, they could sell that stored energy back at a profit.

Standardized software programs that throttle EV charging speeds during peak hours already exist. Drivers can use them if, for example, they want to keep charging costs down by primarily charging their cars during off-peak hours when electricity costs are lower, or if they want to use electricity only from solar power to charge, said Rajit Gadh, a researcher who studies EV charging and scalability at UCLA. But the process for sending energy back to the grid is a different story. Individual manufacturers haven't yet landed on a standard way to tell cars when and how much energy to discharge, Gadh said.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: "What is needed is really [for] every EV charging vendor — and every EV manufacturer, actually — to have this protocol built in, adhere to it in its full specification, and make it available," Gadh told Live Science.

With the right protocols, though, cars of the future will be able to do more than interface with the electrical grid. "Vehicle-to-everything" technologies could enable cars to communicate with infrastructure and other vehicles to avoid traffic and collisions.

Some cars today are already equipped with vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communications. These systems use short-range radio signals to alert other V2V-equipped vehicles of the car's speed, direction of travel and braking patterns. The radio signals can travel about 1,000 feet (300 meters), allowing the vehicle to receive data from cars that are not in the driver's line of sight.

V2V systems could help reduce traffic collisions by warning drivers about oncoming cars they can't see yet — for example, by alerting a driver to another car speeding toward an intersection or coming around a bend as the driver is passing another vehicle on a twisty, two-lane highway. Not all cars have the technology, though, so its practical utility is limited for now.

Some driver assistance technologies, such as lane departure warnings and cruise control, have been on the market in personal cars for decades. These technologies and more recent assistive features require the driver to be in control of the vehicle, but theoretically, they make driving easier. For example, Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised) mode handles most steering and braking tasks, but safe operation requires the driver to keep their eyes on the road and be ready to take over at a moment’s notice. In the next several years, drivers will likely see new features that automate driving in more contexts.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Some of these features will allow drivers to take their attention off the road entirely and enjoy some in-car entertainment, as long as they're alert and able to retake control of the vehicle within a few seconds if conditions change. Technologies that fully automate driving in many circumstances within certain service areas will likely be in about 4% of cars on the market by 2035, according to a white paper from the World Economic Forum.

In cars equipped with these features, "you're still going to have driver controls, but under certain circumstances, it will be effectively an automated vehicle," Luke Neurauter, who leads the Division of Vehicle, Driver and System Safety at the Virginia Tech Transportation Institute, told Live Science.

Mercedes-Benz introduced its Drive Pilot system for two consumer car lines in 2022. On the entire German Autobahn network and on certain freeways between and around Los Angeles, San Francisco and Las Vegas, during heavy traffic, the system lets the driver turn their attention toward other activities, such as reading a book or eating lunch, while the car handles steering and keeping pace with other nearby vehicles.

But as the artificial intelligence (AI) models that control autonomous driving improve and become better able to handle unusual scenarios — often called "edge" or "corner" cases — on the road, drivers will be able to hand over control to their cars in more situations, said Rahul Jain, an electrical and computer engineer at the University of Southern California.

Future AI systems might "have some reasoning ability, and then because of that, it can handle these corner cases much better than current systems are able to do," Jain told Live Science. For example, a car might be able to better respond to an indecisive pedestrian who suddenly enters a crossing, assess whether to enter potentially hazardous conditions such as flooded roads, or safely navigate around unusual circumstances, such as construction work, on a highway.

While some systems will enable drivers to make fewer decisions, others that may roll out in the next several years will track a driver's attention and alert them with sounds, an indicator light or haptic feedback when their focus falters. These systems use cameras and software to track head position, eye movement and steering-wheel input to ensure drivers are focused on the road even when they're using assistive features such as lane centering, Neurauter said.

In addition to looking for distracted driving, the technology might expand to monitor drivers for fatigue and alcohol impairment, he added. That information could then affect "whether or not other features become active, or change how they act, based on the driver state at that moment in time," Neurauter said. Proposed legislation could make this technology a requirement in new vehicles as early as 2027, but technological hurdles and concerns over privacy and false positives could stall its implementation.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The technology could also assist drivers who become unable to safely operate the vehicle — for example, if the driver falls asleep or experiences a medical emergency. If a car detects that the driver is not holding the steering wheel or actively controlling the vehicle, it could send a series of visible, audible, or tactile alerts. If the driver doesn’t respond to those cues, a car might turn on its hazard lights and come to a stop. Some vehicle manufacturers are already rolling out such technology; for example, Volkswagen has made it available in all new vehicles from model year 2025.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: While personal cars may not offer full automation, highly automated car services will become much more common as rideshare vehicles in major metro areas. In some cities, like San Francisco, commuters already rely heavily on autonomous vehicles from Waymo. The company has rolled out its cars in nearly a dozen cities — including Dallas, Houston, Atlanta and Los Angeles — and has announced plans to expand service to more than 20 additional locales. Other companies — such as Nuro and Volkswagen’s MOIA — are testing their vehicles with human drivers on board before rolling out full public service.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Currently, autonomous vehicles navigate by combining information from preloaded, high-resolution maps and real-time radar, lidar and visual data collected by cameras and sensors attached to the car. An onboard computer uses that information to build a 3D map of its surroundings. Right now, the cost of these sensors makes them impractical for consumer vehicles, Jain said, but they’re becoming cheaper as manufacturers scale up production. The cars also use an AI model trained on both common and unusual driving situations to anticipate how other vehicles and pedestrians will behave and plot a safe path forward, Jain added.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Developing those high-resolution maps takes time, which is one of the main reasons autonomous rideshares aren’t available everywhere yet. Mapping usually involves decking out a car with high-end visual sensors and lasers and driving it throughout the region. Although cities like San Francisco have been mapped with this level of precision, much of the U.S. has not.
"It's very difficult to do overnight," said John Dolan, an autonomous-driving researcher at the Carnegie Mellon University Robotics Institute.

Complexities also tend to arise in city environments, where unexpected stops are more common and there are many pedestrians who behave unpredictably or jaywalk. But interstate highway driving doesn't face as many of those obstacles, and that could enable autonomous long-haul drives.

"[Autonomous] trucking, I would expect, would be the first thing that's going to happen" in terms of autonomous travel outside of major cities, Jain said. A few driverless trucks are already on the road: Pittsburgh-based company Aurora deployed the technology on I-45 in Texas, between Dallas and Houston, in 2025, with plans to expand across the southern U.S.
While there's speculation involved in predicting the range of self-driving capabilities available in a decade, the picture for EVs is a little clearer.

Right now, lithium-ion batteries dominate the EV market. Each cell in a lithium-ion battery has two electrodes, commonly a layered graphite electrode and a metal oxide or phosphate electrode, separated by a liquid electrolyte solution. Lithium ions migrate back and forth between these two electrodes when a person charges and discharges the battery.

Many electric cars with lithium-ion batteries can already travel more than 300 miles (480 km) on a charge. But that's not ideal for a long-range car trip, because charging stations are few and far between in the country's vast interior and charging takes longer than filling up a gas tank.

Solid-state batteries, which replace the liquid electrolyte with a solid electrolyte made of ceramic, polymer or sulfide materials, could make that cross-country trip in an EV a practical option, allowing an electric car to travel more than 750 miles (1,200 km) on a single charge. Some prototype battery packs can already achieve this range under controlled conditions. If a solid electrolyte were paired with an anode made of pure lithium, rather than graphite or hard carbon, it would allow the battery to store more energy than a lithium-ion cell of similar mass can.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Solid-state batteries may also enable faster charging. In current batteries that use liquid electrolytes, charging and discharging the battery too quickly can cause dendrites, thin branches of lithium that stretch across the cell and short-circuit the battery. A solid electrolyte could, in theory, block those dendrites, which would enable cars to charge fully in just 10 to 15 minutes. The higher energy density from a lithium metal anode also translates to a greater range than that from a similarly sized lithium-ion battery, Eric Wachsman, director of the Maryland Energy Innovation Institute at the University of Maryland, told Live Science.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Many of the raw materials that go into existing lithium-ion batteries are concentrated in a handful of geographic areas. In 2023, Australia, China and Chile mined about 85% of that year's lithium supply; China mined the majority of graphite used that year as well. And battery materials still make up a significant portion of an electric vehicle's cost.

Sodium-ion batteries could be cheaper and easier to source. Sodium is plentiful in Earth's crust, which means mining could be done throughout the U.S., potentially with a comparatively low environmental impact.

Such batteries also rely on a more widely available electrode material. Sodium ions are larger than lithium ions, so they don't fit in between layers of graphite like lithium ions do. Instead, sodium-ion batteries use hard carbon electrodes.

"When you cook at home and your soup boils over and you get this black ring around your pot, this is hard carbon," Maximilian Fichtner, a solid-state chemist at the Helmholtz Institute Ulm for Electrochemical Energy Storage in Germany, told Live Science. "You can produce this from sucrose or from biomass, from whatever. You can do that everywhere."

The downside is that hard carbon holds less sodium than graphite holds lithium, said Eric McCalla, a battery materials chemist at McGill University in Canada. That means sodium-ion batteries can't store as much energy relative to their mass, and they don't last quite as long as their lithium counterparts.
"The range won't be as large," McCalla told Live Science. "It'll be a fantastic commuter car, but you're not going to go on a family trip from Montreal to California so easily."

Manufacturers are already bringing sodium-ion technology to market. For instance, the Chinese company CATL began mass-producing the batteries in February and claims that their battery packs enable EV ranges over 250 miles (400 km).

But new technologies are being developed rapidly. For example, some scientists are making sodium-ion batteries that use solid electrolytes, combining the higher energy density of solid-state lithium batteries with the cost savings of sodium batteries.

This hybrid battery chemistry is still in the early stages of development, experts told Live Science. "I would be surprised to see them in cars in the next decade," McCalla told Live Science in an email. "I've been surprised before, though."
The future we're describing is the utopian scenario. But the biggest obstacles are likely not technological but rather regulatory, economic, political or cultural, experts said.

"We're going to try to guess at a timeline of when some of these things are going to come in, and odds are, we're going to be wrong," McCalla told Live Science. "Odds are, we're going to be slower than we think."

Solar panels may not wind up being the most economic or practical way to increase EVs' range, while scaling up manufacturing capacity for next-generation batteries is expensive and could slow EV adoption in the U.S. The utility of vehicle-to-vehicle communications, meanwhile, could be limited by a slow rollout and adoption of V2V-equipped cars among drivers.

Whether EVs will be ubiquitous will likely come down to their affordability relative to gas-powered vehicles, which is affected not just by manufacturing and technological advances but also domestic policy choices, such as whether to subsidize EVs or their charging networks.

One challenge for manufacturers is that the automated features drivers prefer may not always be safer. A recent review of automated systems found that those focused on driver safety, such as automatic safety or lane centering, tend to reduce crashes, while those focused on comfort, such as adaptive cruise control, can increase accidents. The authors proposed that such systems make it easier for people to disengage or become distracted while driving and possibly overestimate the capabilities of the system.

paras.en: And there are other kinks to work out for autonomous rideshare vehicles. In December 2025, a horde of Waymos stalled during a power outage, clogging San Francisco intersections. The cars are programmed to treat dark traffic signals as four-way stops, according to a statement from Waymo, but they occasionally ping human operators for confirmation. During the outage, the number of confirmation requests spiked, leading to delayed responses — and lengthy traffic jams. The company says it has since released software updates that allow its vehicles to act more decisively at dark signals. But questions remain about how the fleet will respond in natural disasters, and some have expressed frustration that autonomous rideshare vehicles already slow down ambulances, fire trucks and police cars responding to emergencies.

paras.en: One of the biggest roadblocks to automated driving is the regulatory environment, Neurauter said. Regulations on self-driving vehicles vary by state, and some, such as New York, effectively prohibit driverless vehicles entirely. Where they are legal, they often must carry higher insurance and pass testing, which could limit their rollout.

"When we get into automated driving, the driving behavior is being governed by software that's installed on a computer that's in the vehicle," Steven Shladover, a research engineer at the University of California, Berkeley, told Live Science. "That gets us into a messy gray area where both the federal and the state roles kind of overlap, and that's politically very complicated." For example, different states could end up with different rules for establishing who's legally responsible for an accident involving automated driving.

articles.title: 'October is the ideal time to get vaccinated': Flu season is kicking off early, experts say
articles.author: Olivia Maule

paras.en: Flu season is off to an early start in some parts of the U.S., data shows.

In a typical year, U.S. flu activity starts building in late fall — typically in October or November — and peaks between December and February. This year, flu activity is currently low but rising nationwide: During the week ending Sept. 26, 3.4% of respiratory samples tested by clinical labs were positive for flu, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) data.
That's about seven times the rate that was seen at the same point last year. About 0.5% of samples tested positive during the week ending Sept. 27, 2025.

"This particular year, it appears to be starting early — like right now," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at Vanderbilt Health in Tennessee, told Live Science. Patients at clinics in his area are already testing positive for flu, he said.

The early uptick in flu is mostly unfolding in Western states, including Washington, California and Arizona. In Washington, for example, the share of emergency department visits diagnosed as flu climbed from 0.25% in the week ending Aug. 29 to 1.34% in the week ending Oct. 3, according to CDC emergency department data. That's a more than fivefold increase over six weeks.
Where the flu took off first isn't a warning sign in itself, Schaffner noted.

"There's nothing unusual about flu starting in the West Coast and moving east," he said. Recent seasons have more often begun in the Southeast or Midwest, he noted, but "it can start almost anywhere."
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Nowadays, seasonal flu is caused by three subtypes of flu viruses: two subtypes of influenza A, called H1N1 and H3N2, and the Victoria lineage of influenza B. (A second subtype of influenza B used to circulate but is now thought to be extinct.)

Last season, a fast-spreading version of H3N2 known as subclade K dominated. The CDC classified the 2025-2026 season as highly severe for children, as at least 195 children died of flu-related causes.

Schaffner likens influenza A and B to siblings. "They're very related, but they each have their own individual characteristics," he said. Influenza A strains usually cause the biggest outbreaks early in the season, while influenza B strains "kind of smolder along" and account for most cases toward the end, he noted.

This year, H1N1 has taken the initial lead. Of the influenza A samples that public health labs subtyped during the week ending Sept. 26, 96% were identified as H1N1, according to CDC data. That doesn't mean H1N1 will continue to dominate throughout the season; it just gives a snapshot of what's happening now.

The dominant strain matters because flu is "a moving target," said Dr. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia. The virus constantly mutates — especially hemagglutinin, the protein on the virus's surface that it uses to latch onto human cells. Hemagglutinin is the main target of flu vaccines.

An early start to the season doesn't guarantee it'll be a severe one, either. In its 2026-2027 season outlook, the CDC projected that this season will likely be moderate, although it has only low-to-moderate confidence in that forecast.
Everyone 6 months and older is recommended to get an annual flu vaccine.

Influenza is especially dangerous for children under 5, adults 65 and older, people with chronic health conditions and pregnant people, as these groups are more prone to severe infections. Serious cases of flu can lead to complications such as pneumonia, sepsis, and brain or heart inflammation, and in some cases, they can be deadly. Tens of thousands of people die of flu each season in the U.S.

For flu vaccination, timing matters. The CDC generally doesn't recommend vaccination in July or August for most adults, because the shot's protection can wane over the course of a season. But with flu arriving early, "October is the ideal time to get vaccinated, and even more so right now," Schaffner said.

When circulating strains' features differ from those captured in the vaccine, "that usually predicts a more difficult season," Offit said. That said, it's too early to know if this year's flu shots are a good match for the circulating flu viruses.
Protection begins building right after you get the shot, but it takes up to about two weeks to reach full strength.

How much protection a flu vaccine offers varies by season, depending partly on how well its formulation matches the strains that circulate. Offit said that protection against symptomatic illness varies by age group and that the vaccines are "a little more effective" at preventing more severe illness. In terms of flu cases that prompt people to seek medical care, the shot has been 29% to 56% effective over the past decade, the CDC estimates.

While the vaccines are less reliable at preventing mild cases of flu, Schaffner said, they work best at "keeping you out of the hospital, keeping you out of the intensive care unit, and keeping you out of the cemetery."

The CDC's 2026-2027 guidance keeps its recommendation of an annual flu vaccine for everyone 6 months and older, with high-dose and adjuvanted shots preferred for adults 65 and older. (Adjuvanted shots contain an extra ingredient to help rev up the immune system.)

There's also a new option: In August, the Food and Drug Administration approved mFlusiva, the first mRNA flu vaccine, for adults 50 and older. (You can find out where mFlusiva shots are available near you using Moderna's vaccine finder.) With the mRNA shot, "you're less likely to get symptomatic disease," Offit told Live Science.

Traditional flu shots contain purified pieces of the virus itself, Schaffner explained. With mRNA, the vaccine contains a "blueprint" of those proteins — essentially a set of genetic instructions that the body's cells then use. In mFlusiva's case, those instructions code for hemagglutinin (the protein on the virus's surface that it uses to latch onto human cells) from each of three flu subtypes, Offit said. The mRNA then breaks down in the body, Offit noted. It "cannot influence human genetic material," Schaffner emphasized.

paras.en: Whether this early start gives way to a heavy flu season should become clearer in the coming weeks, as the CDC's weekly surveillance reports will show whether cases keep climbing beyond the West.

Olivia Maule is a science journalist whose beats include space, biotechnology and the environment. She holds a B.A. in biology and a B.S. in anthropology from the University of Florida and completed a master's degree in science communication at U.C. Santa Cruz. A 2025 AAAS Mass Media Fellow, she wrote stories and produced videos during a summer at El Nuevo Día, Puerto Rico's largest newspaper, and has written for Eos, Mongabay, Science magazine and Stanford Report. Olivia is a native Spanish and English speaker.

articles.title: Inuit figurine: A 700-year-old Indigenous carving of a European made a century before Columbus
articles.author: Kristina Killgrove

paras.en: Where it is from: Baffin Island, Nunavut, Canada

This wooden figurine was discovered in 1977 in an early house built by the ancestors of the Inuit on Baffin Island in northern Canada. The unique carving represents a person wearing European clothing and a cross on their chest. Dated to 1350, the figurine is the earliest Indigenous representation of a European anywhere in the Western Hemisphere and probably depicts a Norseman.

The tiny driftwood carving, which is currently on display at the Canadian Museum of History, measures just 2.1 inches (5.4 centimeters) tall. According to the museum, the featureless face and stumpy arms are common in 14th-century Inuit carvings, but the depiction of a non-Inuit is unique.

The mysterious figure wears a long robe or tunic with a cross on the front — a garment that is similar to those worn in the 11th to 13th centuries by Norse Christians from Greenland. The Norse sagas mention a place called "Helluland," which Leif Eriksson (also spelled Erikson) visited in the early 11th century and is most likely Baffin Island.

Around A.D. 1000, Norse explorers landed in what is now Newfoundland and set up camp at a site archaeologists call l'Anse aux Meadows. Wood buildings and remains from iron production are all that is left of the earliest European settlement in the Americas.

The Norse likely made multiple trips from Greenland to Canada over the centuries in order to trade metal and cloth with the Inuit's ancestors, known as the Thule, and procure walrus ivory in return, as European-origin artifacts have been found in early Inuit houses on Baffin Island. But the Norse eventually abandoned their westward trade routes, possibly due to the resistance of the Indigenous people and the long distance.

This wooden figurine may commemorate a meeting between the Inuit and the Norse and is especially important because it was crafted long before sustained contact in the late 15th century, according to the museum. It is also the earliest evidence of the Indigenous perspective of visitors from the east, revealing which characteristics of the Norse the artisan observed and felt were important to depict.
For more stunning archaeological discoveries, check out our Astonishing Artifacts archives.

articles.title: Raised in Apartheid South Africa, 2026 Nobel Peace Prize Winner Navi Pillay Is One of the World’s Leading Human Rights Jurists

paras.en: Navanethem Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize “for her efforts to promote peace and international law.”

The Nobel committee lauded the 85-year-old South African jurist and former United Nations human rights chief for her “commitment to universal legal principles” and her “firm moral compass” throughout her long career.

Through decades of work in South African and international courts, Pillay, who is known as Navi, has helped shape legal efforts to hold governments and individuals accountable for human rights abuses and mass atrocities.

Pillay was born in Durban, South Africa, in 1941. She grew up in a poor family of Indian Tamil descent. The daughter of a bus driver, she pursued a career in law at a time when discrimination limited opportunities for non-white South Africans. She established her own law firm in 1967 and in 1988 became the first South African at Harvard Law School to become a Doctor of Juridical Science, the school’s most advanced degree.

Under apartheid, Pillay and other non-white South Africans were “treated like dirt,” she told the Agence France-Presse (AFP) in 2023. But rather than letting the mistreatment keep her down, she opted to “fight every step of the way.”
“I always had a sense of confidence about who I am and how you confront any kind of discrimination,” she told AFP. “Open your mouth and speak up, condemning it.”

Pillay’s early career centered on defending anti-apartheid activists, including Nelson Mandela, whom she joins as a Nobel Peace Prize laureate. In 1995, she broke another barrier when she became the first non-white woman appointed to South Africa’s High Court.

Her work subsequently took her onto the international stage. In 1999, Pillay became a judge and president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, which investigated crimes committed during the 1994 genocide. During her tenure, she helped establish important legal precedents recognizing sexual violence as potential acts of genocide and crimes against humanity, bringing international attention to the estimated 100,000 to 250,000 Rwandan women who were raped during the three-month massacre.

paras.en: “Rape had always been regarded as one of the spoils of war,” she said at the time. “Now it is a war crime, no longer a trophy of war.”

From 2008 to 2014, Pillay served as the U.N. high commissioner for human rights. From 2021 to 2025, she chaired the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, leading an investigation that concluded Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip. (Israel strongly rejected the report.)

Pillay also served as a judge on the International Criminal Court and currently serves as an ad hoc judge on the International Court of Justice, the U.N.’s primary judicial body, in an ongoing case assessing whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.

By honoring Pillay, the Nobel committee sought to remind the world that international law is the “foundation for a more peaceful world,” Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Nobel committee, said during the award announcement.
“International law has never been perfect,” Frydnes added. But it “sets the standards. Legal measures do prevent acts of war and violence. That is a fact.”

Pillay learned that she had won the prize while attending an international law conference in Courtroom 600 of the Nuremberg Palace of Justice, where top Nazi leaders were indicted and tried for their crimes during World War II.
“At this venue, your applause means a great deal,” she said after hearing the news. “But being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this information.”
Pillay is the first South African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Four South African men—Albert Lutuli, Desmond Tutu, Nelson Mandela and F.W. de Klerk—have received the award.

Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel established the Nobel Peace Prize, as well as prizes for physiology or medicine, chemistry, literature and physics, with a bequest in his will, which he drafted in 1895. The prizes were first awarded in 1901. The economics prize was established in Nobel’s memory in 1968.

This year, the Nobel Peace Prize celebrates its 125th anniversary, with 287 individuals and organizations nominated for the award. The committee noted that the 2026 prize “springs directly” from Nobel’s will, which stated that the award should be given to those who have “conferred the greatest benefit to humankind.”

Pillay is “one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time,” according to the committee. “[Her] commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.”

articles.title: A Digital Swamp Coming to New York City’s MoMA Is 'Made to Envelop You' in Nature With the Help of Cutting-Edge Technology

paras.en: A new-age swamp is bubbling up inside the lobby of New York City’s Museum of Modern Art (MoMA). Beginning next week, visitors will find themselves stepping through a colorful, pulsing digital ecosystem that may seem a world away from the city’s urbanity and frenetic pace.

“Wetland,” an immersive exhibition by the Danish artist Jakob Kudsk Steensen, thrives in this sensory disconnect. Opening on October 12, MoMA’s newest show is a futuristic, digital vision of nature. It also opens a portal back to the mucky landscapes that major cities—including New York—were founded upon.
The installation harnesses macro photogrammetry and game-engine software (the architecture behind video games) to simulate the movements, sounds and sights of a large-scale swamp.

Wall-spanning screens display photographs and 3D scans of real-life wetlands. Digitally altered field recordings of amphibians and susurrating riverine rhythms have been mixed with human vocals, including those from the Venezuelan musician Arca.
“At MoMA, it’s made to envelop you—but with a sense of … dance,” Kudsk Steensen tells the New York Times’ Frank Rose. “Things appear. They vanish. They’re dark. They’re bright. They’re vocal.”
“Wetland” features just a single work of art: the simulated swamp installation known as Berl-Berl, which Kudsk Steensen has allowed to evolve since its creation in 2021.

Both Berl-Berl’s form and name were inspired by the swamps surrounding Berlin, many of which have fallen victim to urban development. The artist collaborated with Berlin’s natural history museum to devote months to studying the landscape. A combination of photography, sound recording, kayaking, swamp-slogging and archival research left Kudsk Steensen with a trove of material documenting humanity’s relationship with wetland habitats. The result was Berl-Berl, first installed in Berghain, a nightclub located in a sprawling decommissioned East German power plant.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “In the beginning, I thought I was just making an immersive show, with some nature sounds, some screens and some things that are moving around,” Kudsk Steensen told Dazed’s Juule Kay in 2021, ahead of Berl-Berl’s debut. “But when I walked around in the space, I started to whistle and clap and noticed the echo.”

Each iteration of the installation—in Denmark, South Korea, Switzerland and elsewhere in Berlin—remains in a state of flux. At times, folklore plays a central role. Triglav, a three-headed god from Slavic folklore, makes an appearance at MoMA in the form of a giant tree. Although absent from the MoMA iteration, the shape-shifting water spirit Nøkken, who is said to appear to travelers as a handsome, music-playing young man, often appears in the digital swamp, too.

“We used to sing to the world in order to navigate it,” Kudsk Steensen said in 2024. “And in Europe, in the past, there were many practices to create songs as ways of mapping terrains, especially rivers and swamps, because these are ever-changing landscapes.”
- In July, the United Nations added the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge, which protects a swamp sprawled between Florida and Georgia, to its list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
- UNESCO described it as a “diverse mosaic of wetlands, savannas and forests” with stunning biodiversity.

In “Wetland,” Kudsk Steensen uses macro photogrammetry—the practice of turning microscopic details into larger images—to illuminate and archive the overlooked textures of wetland soils, plants and currents. Cutting-edge tools help bring the artist closer to nature instead of dividing him from it. “Technology for me, in the sense of being a medium, is a connector,” the artist has said.

“It’s fascinating,” Paola Antonelli, MoMA’s senior curator of architecture and design, tells the Times. “This most technological part of the museum is the one that really digs into nature, into consciousness.”
“Wetland” will be on view at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City from October 12, 2026, to March 7, 2027.

articles.title: Watch Five Adorable Newborn Cheetah Cubs Grow on a Livestream From the Smithsonian's Conservation Biology Institute

paras.en: Safe in their den, a new litter of cheetah cubs curls up for nap time. One extends an arm and leg in a big stretch, and another stumbles over its siblings to nurse. Five tiny bodies are piled together, one black-spotted coat blending into another.

In a milestone for cheetah conservation, the five cubs were born on October 5 at the Smithsonian’s Conservation Biology Institute in Front Royal, Virginia. When they’re not snoozing, the healthy, young cats are active—they started climbing on their mother on day one.

“Because there’s five of them, somebody’s usually nursing,” Adrienne Crosier, a cheetah biologist and curator of carnivores at the Conservation Biology Institute, tells Smithsonian magazine. “Somebody’s always hungry. Somebody always needs to be groomed. Somebody always needs a bath.”

Zura, who at 5 years old is a first-time mother, has taken it all in stride. She’s an incredibly calm and attentive parent, and she’s dedicating almost every moment of her time to the cubs. Today, she ventured out of the den to get a bite to eat for the first time since their birth.
“That’s very, very normal,” Crosier explains. “But we obviously were happy that she came out, got some food, got some water, and then she went right back to the den with the cubs.”

Born with their eyes closed and ears shut, cheetah cubs are completely dependent on their mothers for survival. It typically takes about four to seven days before they open their eyes, and their ears—initially “flat against their little heads,” Crosier says—will stand up days later.

For now, the care staff is hands-off with the cubs, letting the feline family bond without interference. But they’re keeping a close eye on the cheetah cub cam, which shows scenes from within the den. The online live stream also gives viewers around the world a special window into the animals’ lives, especially since the Front Royal facility is closed to the public.

The cubs will grow rapidly as they nurse. They’ll put on about 50 grams of weight daily—something between a golf ball and an egg. After about three or four weeks, they’ll start to grow curious when Zura leaves the den to eat or drink, gathering at the door when she exits. “They’re going to want to start following her outside,” Crosier says.

Eventually, animal care staff will come into the den and look at the cheetahs to make sure they seem healthy. They’ll pick up a cub, bring it outside to a scale to get its weight, then deposit it back with the family a few minutes later. Staff will mark each baby with a small shave mark in the fur so that they can tell them all apart. At six weeks, they’ll have their first vet exam and vaccinations, and they’ll get transponders implanted for more reliable identification.

Zura herself was born at the institute in 2021, and her mother and grandmother are also at the facility. With the newest litter, that makes four generations of the family in the biologists’ care. The cubs’ 9-year-old father, Flash, also at the institute, has sired seven cubs from previous litters. Cheetah fathers are not involved with raising the youngsters.

Cheetahs are listed as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, and their global population has plunged by more than 90 percent since 1900. Human activity has fragmented their wild populations, but the cats had been struggling with low genetic diversity since around the end of the last ice age, when an extinction event drove several cheetah species to disappear.

The Conservation Biology Institute breeds cheetahs in accordance with the Cheetah Species Survival Plan, established by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums. Through this initiative, ten facilities across the country select which cheetahs should breed together based on their DNA, temperament, health and other factors. Careful “matchmaking,” which sometimes involves cheetahs traveling hundreds of miles between facilities to meet their possible mate, aims to promote genetic diversity in the population and “produce offspring with the best possible chance of living a healthy life,” per the Smithsonian.
